sentences.text: This dinosaur is identified by a unique feature: its front neck vertebrae possess split spines, a trait rarely seen in its group.
The known skeleton includes the atlas, axis, and seven other neck bones, though one piece is absent from the collection.
Its breastbone is substantial, measuring roughly 530 mm long, with reinforced edges and a pronounced side margin.
The genus name Erketu honors Erketü tengri, the creator god of Mongolian shamanism.
The specific name ellisoni commemorates Mick Ellison, a senior paleoartist and friend of Mark Norell.
Remains of this animal were uncovered between 2002 and 2003 by a team from the American Museum of Natural History working with Mongolian scientists.
The primary specimen, known as the holotype, came from the Bor Guvé site inside the Bayan Shireh Formation.
Daniel T. Ksepka and Mark Norell formally named the species Erketu ellisoni in 2006.
Its exceptionally long neck suggests it fed high up in vegetation.
Taxonomically, Erketu falls within the Saurischia class.
It is placed in the family Euhelopodidae and is viewed as a close relative of Euhelopus.
A 2017 study grouped it in a polytomy with Chubutisaurus inside the Somphospondyli.
It inhabited a landscape shaped by rivers and lakes within a semi-arid climate.
The animal lived during the Cenomanian to Coniacian stages, estimated to be between 95.9 ± 6.0 and 89.6 ± 4.0 million years ago.
